gaps.sentence: Students ___ to buy the textbook; copies are available in the library.
gaps.explanation: 'Don't have to' plus the infinitive expresses absence of obligation: don't have to buy.

gaps.sentence: In this lab, food and drink ___ be brought past the reception area.
gaps.explanation: Written prohibitions use 'must not': must not be brought.

gaps.sentence: You ___ better take some cash — the stall does not take cards.
gaps.explanation: 'Had better' warns about a sensible action: had better take.

gaps.sentence: You ___ have seen a ghost — there is no such thing!
gaps.hint: a past claim rejected as impossible
gaps.explanation: 'Can't have' rejects a past claim as impossible: can't have seen.

gaps.sentence: ___ I get you something from the shop while I am out?
gaps.hint: making an offer with shall I
gaps.explanation: 'Shall I' offers to do something: Shall.

gaps.sentence: Her car is not in the car park and her office light is off, so she ___ home.
gaps.hint: a confident conclusion about the past
gaps.explanation: A confident conclusion about the past uses 'must have' plus the participle: must have gone.

gaps.sentence: Visitors ___ to leave the gallery by 6 p.m.
gaps.hint: have to takes the full infinitive
gaps.explanation: 'Have to' takes the full infinitive with 'to': have to leave.

gaps.sentence: Visitors ___ leave any bags unattended; security removes them at once.
gaps.explanation: 'Must not' expresses prohibition; 'need not' would mean it is optional.
